paragraphs.heading: What a desert climate is
paragraphs.text: A desert climate, also called an arid climate, is a dry type of climate where evaporation runs far ahead of precipitation. In the Köppen climate classification it carries the codes BWh and BWk. The ground in these places is usually bare rock or sand that holds little water, so what little rain falls dries off quickly. The hot kind, BWh, covers about 14.2% of Earth's land, more than any other Köppen type.

paragraphs.heading: How a place qualifies
paragraphs.text: To decide whether a place is arid, you first work out a precipitation threshold for it. If its yearly precipitation is under half that threshold, it counts as desert, written BW; between half and the full threshold, it is semi-arid instead. Most deserts get somewhere between 25 and 200 mm of rain in a year. A few very hot areas in Central Australia, the Sahel and the Guajira Peninsula still count as arid with as much as 430 mm, because evaporation there is so extreme. A mean annual temperature of 18 °C then splits hot deserts (BWh), above it, from cold deserts (BWk), below it.

paragraphs.heading: Hot deserts
paragraphs.text: Hot deserts usually sit under the subtropical ridge, often between 20° and 33° of latitude north and south. There, calm sinking air and high pressure overhead sweep away clouds, giving hot, dry weather and strong sunshine. They stretch across North Africa, West Asia, interior Australia and the southwestern United States, among other places, and appear on every continent except Antarctica. The hottest month usually averages 29 to 35 °C, and midday readings of 43 to 46 °C are common. Death Valley's 56.7 °C is currently considered the highest temperature recorded on Earth, yet in the cooler months desert nights can fall to freezing or below as heat escapes through the clear sky.

paragraphs.heading: Cold deserts
paragraphs.text: Cold deserts (BWk) usually have hot or warm dry summers, though not as hot as in hot deserts, and cold, dry winters. They tend to lie at higher altitudes than hot deserts and are usually drier. Many sit in the 30s and 40s of latitude, often in a rain shadow: the downwind side of high mountains that block rain carried by westerly winds. The Patagonian Desert in Argentina, with the Andes to its west, is one example. The Gobi in northern China and Mongolia is another, hot in summer but with the freezing winters of the rest of Inner Asia.

paragraphs.heading: The driest places
paragraphs.text: No part of Earth is known for certain to get no rain at all. Over 17 years, the Atacama Desert in northern Chile averaged only 5 mm of rain a year. Kufra, Libya, in the Sahara, records even less, 0.86 mm a year. Death Valley's official station reports 60 mm a year, but across 40 months between 1931 and 1934 only 16 mm fell there.

paragraphs.heading: Deserts at the poles
paragraphs.text: Some parts of the Arctic and Antarctic, called polar deserts, also get very little precipitation, since the cold, dry air freezes most of it. These areas share some desert features, such as streams that flow only now and then, very salty lakes and bare land wherever there is no ice, as in the McMurdo Dry Valleys of Antarctica. Even so, they are normally classed as polar climates, because their summers average below 10 °C.
